# What changes does FlashAttention-2 make to the FlashAttention algorithm, and what speedup results?

> **ANSWERED**
> Evidence-sufficiency score 1.00 (heuristic)
> _Uncalibrated: decided by the heuristic scorer, not a fitted model._

## Answer

FlashAttention‑2 revises the original FlashAttention pipeline by reshaping how work is divided among GPU resources. *[unverified]* First, the algorithm is altered to cut the number of non‑matrix‑multiply floating‑point operations, which were a dominant source of overhead in the earlier design [1]. *[partially supported]* Second, attention is parallelized across multiple thread blocks even when a single head is processed, raising occupancy and allowing more of the GPU’s compute units to stay busy [1]. Third, within each thread block the workload is spread among warps, which reduces the amount of data that must pass through shared memory and therefore lowers intra‑block communication costs [1].

These three engineering changes directly address the sub‑optimal work partitioning that limited the original FlashAttention to only 25‑40 % of the theoretical FLOPs / s on A100 GPUs and prevented it from matching the efficiency of dense GEMM kernels [2][3]. *[partially supported]* The original method relied on tiling and an online soft‑max to cut memory traffic, delivering 2‑4× wall‑clock speedups over baseline attention implementations but still falling short of GEMM performance [4]. *[partially supported]*

By applying the new partitioning strategy, FlashAttention‑2 doubles the effective throughput of the baseline FlashAttention implementation, achieving roughly a 2× speedup and reaching 50‑73 % of the theoretical maximum FLOPs / s on A100 hardware, which is close to the efficiency of optimized matrix‑multiply operations [1]. In end‑to‑end GPT‑style training this translates to up to 225 TFLOPs / s per A100 GPU, corresponding to a model‑level FLOPs utilization of about 72 % [1].
